title: The Forbidden City Isn't Flat — That's the Drainage | China Travel Expert
description:
Beijing's Forbidden City looks dead level — but it isn't. The whole palace tilts gently from north to south, and that hidden slope is how it has shed six centuries of rain without a single pump.

The northern Gate of Divine Might stands about 46.05 m above sea level; the Meridian Gate at the south sits at about 44.28 m — a fall of nearly two metres across roughly a kilometre of courtyards. Rain that lands on the marble terraces simply runs downhill, into the Inner Golden Water River and out to the moat. One honest caveat: the palace's dense walls and halls do slow that natural run-off, so the ditches and the carved dragon-head spouts do real work too.

★ Expert Tip: come on a rainy day. That's when you can actually watch the water move south across the courtyards and pour from the dragon-head spouts.

故宫看着是平的，其实不平：北高南低，北边神武门约 46.05 米，南边午门约 44.28 米，近一公里的院落落差不到两米，雨水顺坡自己往南流进内金水河、再入护城河。连 600 年没被淹过。你之前会以为它是平的吗？

Facts verified 2026-11-20:
• The Forbidden City's ground falls from the ~46.05 m north gate (Gate of Divine Might) to the ~44.28 m Meridian Gate in the south — nearly 2 m — letting rainwater drain south by gravity: China Daily, "Forbidden City free of waterlogging" 2016-07-22 https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2016-07/22/content_26183948.htm
• The north-higher-than-south slope sheds rain by gravity into the Inner Golden Water River and the moat (a smaller figure of 1.22 m is also cited): TravelChinaGuide, "Amazing Drainage System of the Forbidden City" https://www.travelchinaguide.com/attraction/beijing/forbidden-city/drainage-system.htm
